key_terms.meaning: Main spanwise beam of a wing; its caps (upper and lower flanges) take bending and its web takes shear.
Chordwise member that holds the wing's shape, supports the skin and stringers, and passes load into the spars.
Small longitudinal stiffener riveted to the skin; it carries axial bending stress and stops the skin buckling.
Heavy longitudinal fuselage member, often a main bending member, stronger than a stringer.
Outer sheet that takes air pressure, shear and part of the bending; in a thin-wing it also forms the torsion box.
A heavy transverse member that closes a section, carries concentrated loads, or holds cabin pressure.
Transverse fuselage ring that keeps the cross-section shape and supports stringers and skin.
Transverse beam under the cabin floor that carries floor and passenger loads into the frames.
Extra plate riveted around a cut-out or joint to replace the strength removed by the hole.
Local machined or forged part that joins one member to another and spreads a concentrated load.
Construction in which the skin alone carries all load; strong but needs a thick, heavy skin.
Skin plus frames, stringers and longerons; thin skin takes shear and pressure, stringers take bending.
Closed cell formed by front spar, rear spar, top and bottom skin; resists wing twisting.
Two thin stiff faces separated by a light core, giving high bending stiffness at low weight.
Hexagonal-cell core of foil or paper sheet; its cell walls carry shear between the faces.
The largest load expected in service; the structure must carry it with no permanent damage.
Limit load × factor of safety (usually 1.5); the structure must not fail at this load.
Ratio of total lift to weight, n = L/W; n = 1 in level flight, higher in a pull-out or gust.
Plot of load factor n against speed V, bounded by stall, structural and gust limits; its corners size the wing.
Circumferential pressure stress in a thin cylinder, σ = p·r/t, with p pressure, r radius, t wall thickness.

takeaways: Every aircraft member is a load path: it collects load from a wider area and hands it to a stronger member until the load reaches a support.
Monocoque skins must be thick to avoid buckling, so real aircraft are semi-monocoque, with stringers taking bending and thin skin taking shear.
A wing behaves as a torsion box and a cantilever beam; ribs keep the box shape and transfer skin loads to the spars.
Sandwich panels give very high bending stiffness for low weight because the faces carry bending and the core carries shear.
Material choice is a trade of strength, stiffness, density, fatigue, temperature, corrosion and cost, never a single property.
Fabrication and joints decide real strength; a riveted or bonded joint, not the plate, is usually the weak point.
Limit load is the worst service load, ultimate load is 1.5 times it, and load factor n = L/W converts flight loads to design loads.
The V-n diagram corners, at maximum manoeuvre and maximum gust at design speeds, give the critical wing bending cases.
Shear force and bending moment along a wing come from integrating the net spanwise load, giving maximum bending moment at the root.
A pressurised fuselage is a beam and a pressure vessel at once; hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, and each flight adds a fatigue cycle.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine labelled sketches of structure, the load path through each member, and a calculation using limit/ultimate load, load factor, the V-n diagram or a shear force and bending moment integration.

bank.q: Define monocoque and semi-monocoque construction. Explain why the semi-monocoque is used for almost all modern aircraft.
outline: Monocoque: skin carries all load, needs great thickness to resist buckling, so it is heavy
Semi-monocoque: thin skin on frames, stringers and longerons
Skin takes shear, torsion and pressure; stringers and longerons take axial bending stress
Frames keep the cross-section shape and shorten the buckling length of the skin
Result: higher strength-to-weight and easier production

bank.q: State the function of a spar, rib, stringer, longeron, frame and bulkhead, and give one place on the aircraft where each is found.
outline: Spar: spanwise beam in the wing, caps take bending, web takes shear
Rib: chordwise member, keeps aerofoil shape, transfers skin load to spars
Stringer: longitudinal skin stiffener, takes axial stress with the skin
Longeron: heavy longitudinal fuselage member carrying bending
Frame: transverse ring maintaining fuselage section and supporting stringers
Bulkhead: transverse member closing the section; pressure bulkhead holds cabin pressure
Each answer tied to a location such as wing box, cabin floor or nose

bank.q: Define limit load, ultimate load, factor of safety and load factor. State the usual values used in aircraft design and explain what each means physically.
outline: Limit load: maximum expected in service, no permanent deformation
Ultimate load = limit load × factor of safety, typically 1.5
Factor of safety accounts for uncertainty in load and material data
Load factor n = L/W, ratio of lift to weight
n = 1 in steady level flight, n = 2.5 typical manoeuvre limit for transport aircraft
Load factor and safety factor convert flight loads into design loads

bank.q: Describe a typical wing structure and trace the path taken by the lift force from skin to wing root.
outline: Aerodynamic suction and pressure on the skin
Skin panels carry the load to stringers and ribs
Ribs distribute load into the front and rear spars
Spar caps take axial bending stress, spar webs take shear
Spars are joined at the root to the centre wing box by fittings
Root bending moment and shear pass into fuselage frames
Sketch showing front spar, rear spar, ribs, stringers and skin

bank.q: A wing has an elliptical or given spanwise lift distribution. Treating the wing as a cantilever, derive the shear force and bending moment at a root station.
outline: Define spanwise load w(y) in N/m, span b, semi-span s
Shear force V(y) = integral of w from the tip to y
Bending moment M(y) = integral of V from the tip to y
Root values: total lift W = area under w(y)
For elliptic loading, root moment is finite and computed by integration
Sketch of shear force and bending moment diagrams, zero at tips
State units: V in N, M in N·m

bank.q: For a given set of design speeds and load factor limits, draw the manoeuvre V-n diagram and identify the corner points that must be used for wing sizing.
outline: Axes: speed V on x, load factor n on y
Stall boundary n = V²/(stall-related) curving from VA to the stall speed
Positive limit n at points A to D, negative limit below the axis
Design cruising and dive speeds VC and VD marked
Gust lines of increasing slope drawn from VC
Corner points: positive manoeuvre at VA and VD, negative manoeuvre, gust intersections
Each corner is a load case for wing bending and torsion

bank.q: A sandwich panel with face thickness t and core thickness c is compared with a solid sheet of the same material and the same weight. Show why the sandwich is far stiffer in bending.
outline: Bending stiffness per unit width proportional to E·t·c²/2 for the sandwich (faces far from the neutral axis)
Solid sheet stiffness proportional to E·t_solid³/12
Same weight means solid thickness equals the total face material
Faces carry direct tension and compression, core carries shear
Core must resist crushing and shear, faces must not wrinkle
Numerical ratio improves as c increases
Practical limit: core shear failure and face wrinkling before bending failure

bank.q: A circular fuselage of radius r and skin thickness t is pressurised to a cabin differential pressure p and also carries a bending moment M. Compute the skin stresses and state which one drives the fatigue life.
outline: Hoop stress σ_h = p·r/t
Longitudinal pressure stress σ_l = p·r/(2t)
Bending stress from σ = M·y/I, with I from the stiffened section
Superpose pressure and bending stresses at top and bottom of the section
Maximum compressive stress on the upper skin must be below buckling stress
Pressure stress cycles once per flight, so it drives fatigue and crack growth
Crack stoppers and doublers limit damage

bank.q: Explain how a riveted lap joint in a fuselage skin carries load, and list the failure modes an engineer checks in its design.
outline: Load travels from one sheet into rivets by bearing and then into the second sheet
Rivet shear, sheet bearing, sheet net-section tension
Row-by-row load transfer; first row takes most load
Hole reduces net area and creates stress concentration
Fatigue cracking from hole edges under repeated pressurisation
Multiple rows, sealant and bonding (rivet-bond) reduce load per rivet
Check against ultimate load with factor 1.5

bank.q: Compare aluminium alloy, titanium alloy and carbon fibre composite for a wing upper skin. Justify a choice and state the trade-offs involved.
outline: Properties table: density, modulus, strength, fatigue, temperature, corrosion, cost
Specific strength and specific stiffness used for fair comparison
Aluminium: cheap, easy to form and rivet, good fatigue if designed, corrodes
Titanium: high temperature and corrosion resistance, high strength, costly and hard to machine
Composites: high specific stiffness, tailorable, no corrosion, poor at bearing and impact, need bonded or bolted joints, higher inspection cost
Choice depends on load case, temperature, environment and production volume
Sensible conclusion, not a single-property ranking

bank.q: A semi-monocoque fuselage is cut for a cargo door. Analyse the effect on the structure, and evaluate the role of doublers, frames and crack stoppers in restoring strength.
outline: Cut-out removes skin area, so the load path is diverted
Stress concentration at corners; corner radii reduce it
Doublers replace lost skin area and spread load into the surrounding skin
Additional frames at the cut-out edges carry the diverted shear
Pressure loads need a pressure-tight door and a reinforced frame
Crack stoppers and tear straps limit damage growth from the opening
Comparison of strength with the uncut structure and fatigue check

bank.q: Using the corners of the V-n diagram and a spanwise load distribution, size the wing root spar caps and evaluate how a change in limit load factor or aspect ratio alters the design.
outline: Obtain design load factor from the V-n diagram corners including gust cases
Lift = n·W, apply factor of safety 1.5 for ultimate load
Convert lift to spanwise load and integrate for root shear and bending moment
Root moment is shared between front and rear spar caps
Cap area from σ = M/(A·d) with d the distance between caps
Check compression cap for buckling and fatigue life at limit load
Raising n increases moment and cap area roughly in proportion
Higher aspect ratio at the same wing area raises root moment

bank.q: Describe how loads from the tail unit are transferred into the rear fuselage, and analyse why the rear fuselage is often critical for bending and fatigue.
outline: Tail plane lift and elevator load produce bending of the rear fuselage
Fin side load and rudder load produce torsion and lateral bending
These enter through fittings and a reinforced frame or bulkhead
Tail load acts at a long lever arm from the centre of gravity
Large bending moments occur in the rear fuselage with less material than the wing box
Fatigue from gust and manoeuvre cycles concentrates at joints and cut-outs
Stiffening by stringers and frames raises buckling strength

glossary.def: The continuous route by which a force travels from where it is applied to the support that reacts it.
A transverse wall-like member that closes a section, carries concentrated load, or holds cabin pressure.
A transverse ring in the fuselage that maintains the cross-section shape and supports stringers and skin.
A small longitudinal stiffener on the inside of the skin that takes axial stress and delays skin buckling.
A heavy longitudinal fuselage member that acts as a main bending member.
The upper or lower flange of a spar, farthest from the neutral axis, carrying the largest bending stress.
A chordwise wing member that gives the aerofoil shape and transfers skin and stringer loads to the spars.
An extra plate added around a cut-out or joint to restore the strength taken away.
A local machined or forged component that connects two members and spreads a concentrated load.
Construction where the skin alone carries all loads, with no internal skeleton.
Construction with thin skin supported by frames, stringers and longerons so that each carries part of the load.
A closed cell of spars and skin that resists twisting of a wing or tail surface.
Two thin stiff faces bonded to a thick light core to obtain high bending stiffness at low weight.
A core of hexagonal cells, made from foil or paper, whose walls carry shear between the faces.
The maximum load expected in service, which the structure must carry without permanent damage.
Limit load multiplied by the factor of safety, usually 1.5; the structure must not fail at this value.
The ratio n = L/W of lift to weight, which measures how many times the aircraft feels heavier than its weight.
A graph of load factor against equivalent airspeed showing the flight envelope and the critical design cases.
The extra lift created when the aircraft meets an upward or downward air current.
The circumferential tensile stress in a pressurised cylinder, equal to p·r/t.
The line in a beam section where bending stress is zero and about which the bending stresses balance.
Sudden sideways deflection of a thin member under compression at a load below its crushing strength.
Failure by repeated load cycles that start and grow a crack at a stress concentration.
Design in which a crack or failed member is stopped by other members until it is found in inspection.
